disclaimer: Suggested stakeholders and contextual factors are prompts for instructor consideration. Applicability depends on the specific engineering problem, activity, or project.

dimensions.Stakeholders: Who uses, operates, maintains, buys, regulates, or is otherwise affected by an engineering system?
dimensions.Public Health: Could the technology affect human health even without an immediate accident? In EE, consider exposure to RF fields, heat, noise, or battery materials where relevant.
dimensions.Safety: Could a fault, failure, or incorrect use injure someone, damage equipment, or create hazardous operation?
dimensions.Welfare: Does the system dependably support people's normal activities, essential services, accessibility, or quality of life? In EE, this often means trustworthy measurements and continuity of power or communication.
dimensions.Global: Does the decision depend on international compatibility, standards, spectrum allocation, supply chains, or deployment across countries?
dimensions.Cultural: Could language, local practices, expectations, or acceptance change how the technology should be designed or used?
dimensions.Social: How does the technology affect groups, communities, accessibility, inclusion, or everyday interaction?
dimensions.Environmental: What energy, materials, emissions, waste, land, or other resources does the system use or affect?
dimensions.Economic: What are the direct purchase, operating, maintenance, replacement, and lifecycle cost trade-offs?
dimensions.Socioeconomic: Do income, location, infrastructure, or social circumstances cause different groups to receive different benefits or burdens from the same technical decision?

courses.title: Introduction to Circuits
courses.rationale: Use a basic circuit or laboratory setup to discuss measurement, safe operation, and the people who rely on the result.

stakeholders.name: Student laboratory users
stakeholders.need: Clear operating limits and safe measurement points
stakeholders.why: They connect circuits and meters, so unclear limits or misleading readings affect their learning and safety.

stakeholders.name: Laboratory technicians
stakeholders.why: They prepare and repair the benches, and need faults to be visible before the next class uses the equipment.

stakeholders.name: Equipment users
stakeholders.why: They may make a design decision from the indicated voltage or current.

stakeholders.name: Course instructors
stakeholders.why: They need a repeatable setup so students can compare results rather than troubleshoot inconsistent equipment.

factors.consideration: Contact with energized circuits, incorrect connections, and component heating.
factors.implication: Consider current limits, isolation, and a safe test procedure.
factors.example: A student moves a lead while a breadboard supply is energized.
factors.teachingIdea: Demonstrate a safer sequence for wiring, energizing, and measuring a simple circuit.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare two probe-and-wiring plans and justify which better prevents an accidental short or contact with an energized point.

factors.consideration: Measurement errors can lead to an unreliable circuit decision.
factors.implication: Specify an acceptable measurement tolerance and verify it.
factors.example: Two voltmeters give different readings on the same resistor network; one varies between trials.
factors.teachingIdea: Have students repeat a voltage measurement and discuss who would rely on its result.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare a cheaper but less repeatable meter with a more reliable one, identify who relies on the reading, and explain one consequence of an incorrect value.

factors.consideration: Component ratings and replacement costs affect practical circuit choices.
factors.implication: Compare suitable components against an instructional budget.
factors.example: A low-cost resistor operates close to its power rating and needs frequent replacement.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare component price with power rating and expected replacement effort.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between two resistor ratings for a given circuit and justify the choice using purchase and replacement cost.

factors.consideration: Foreseeable misuse of a laboratory supply or probe may expose a person to electrical hazards.
factors.implication: Document safe operating limits and supervision needs.
factors.example: An exposed supply terminal is touched during foreseeable laboratory misuse.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a short lab-safety scenario to distinguish a health exposure from ordinary circuit performance.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify one foreseeable misuse of a laboratory supply and propose an operating limit or barrier that reduces exposure.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Pause at a circuit demonstration and ask who would be affected if the displayed voltage were wrong or a lead were unsafe.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify the laboratory user and technician in a measurement setup and derive one safe-use requirement for each.

courses.title: Circuit Analysis
courses.rationale: Connect analytical assumptions to real loads, supply quality, and decisions about circuit operation.

stakeholders.name: Circuit designers
stakeholders.need: Models that represent expected operating conditions
stakeholders.why: They choose models and assumptions that later determine component ratings and load behavior.

stakeholders.name: Equipment operators
stakeholders.why: They see the effect when a real circuit does not hold the expected voltage.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance personnel
stakeholders.why: They need measurements that help locate a fault rather than obscure it.

stakeholders.name: Connected equipment users
stakeholders.need: Power quality that does not disrupt their equipment
stakeholders.why: Their devices may be disrupted by a disturbance produced elsewhere on the shared supply.

factors.consideration: Fault currents and overstressed components may create unsafe operating conditions.
factors.implication: Check worst-case currents and component ratings.
factors.example: A shorted branch draws more current than a selected component can withstand.
factors.teachingIdea: Work a worst-case current calculation before discussing protection.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to calculate fault current for a simple network and select a justified component rating or protective limit.

factors.consideration: Voltage variation or disturbances may interrupt a supplied function.
factors.implication: Define a voltage-quality or continuity constraint for the load.
factors.example: A brief supply sag resets a sensitive control board.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare ideal circuit analysis with a measured voltage-disturbance trace.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set a voltage tolerance for a load and explain what happens to its user when the supply falls below it.

factors.consideration: Oversizing and losses can change the cost of an otherwise valid circuit.
factors.implication: Compare lifecycle cost alongside electrical performance.
factors.example: A larger component lowers losses but costs more initially.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare two circuit designs using purchase cost and expected operating energy.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between two components using both initial cost and annual loss, stating the assumed duty cycle.

factors.consideration: Circuit losses turn supplied energy into heat.
factors.implication: Estimate losses for a representative operating case.
factors.example: A high-current path wastes power as heat over many operating hours.
factors.teachingIdea: Calculate I²R loss for two wiring or load choices.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to estimate energy lost in two circuit alternatives and explain how the difference affects heat and resource use.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Trace a supply disturbance through a circuit and ask which user sees the first practical consequence.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to name two users affected by a voltage sag and derive one circuit-level constraint for each.

courses.title: Electronic Fundamentals
courses.rationale: Use an electronic device or radio-enabled product to examine user exposure, interference, and repairability.

stakeholders.name: Device users
stakeholders.why: They interact with the product and experience its faults or unclear indicators.

stakeholders.name: Test engineers
stakeholders.why: They must show that emissions and immunity claims are supported by repeatable measurements.

stakeholders.name: Nearby equipment users
stakeholders.why: Their devices may malfunction when the new product emits interference.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance technicians
stakeholders.why: They diagnose failures and need accessible, safely serviceable assemblies.

stakeholders.name: Equipment manufacturers
stakeholders.why: They must build a practical design whose reliability and test needs are clear.

factors.consideration: Device faults or thermal stress may affect a person handling the circuit.
factors.implication: Identify a fault response and a temperature limit.
factors.example: A failed transistor causes a board area to overheat.
factors.teachingIdea: Walk through a component-fault case and locate the thermal hazard.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify a likely fault on a simple device and specify one protective response or temperature limit.

factors.consideration: Electromagnetic interference may reduce dependable operation.
factors.implication: Set an immunity or emissions test condition.
factors.example: A nearby transmitter causes a product to reset during use.
factors.teachingIdea: Demonstrate or discuss an EMC susceptibility example.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose an immunity test and state what user-visible behavior would count as an unacceptable failure.

factors.consideration: Device choice influences production and repair cost.
factors.implication: Compare replacement and repair options with performance.
factors.example: A sealed module is inexpensive to buy but costly to replace after one failed part.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare a repairable and non-repairable board over a plausible service life.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare module replacement cost with component-level repair and justify a design choice.

factors.consideration: Quiescent power and short device life add energy use and e-waste.
factors.implication: Measure idle power and consider component replacement.
factors.example: Standby current from many deployed devices adds substantial annual energy demand.
factors.teachingIdea: Measure or estimate idle power and scale it to a fleet.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to calculate annual standby energy for two device designs and recommend one with a reason.

factors.consideration: Controls and indicators may be difficult for some users to understand.
factors.implication: Test a clear indication of normal and fault states.
factors.example: A single flashing LED gives users no clear distinction between normal and fault states.
factors.teachingIdea: Ask students to interpret two indicator schemes without instructions.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to redesign status feedback so a user can distinguish a recoverable fault from normal operation.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Use a small electronic product and ask what its user, test engineer, and nearby device user each needs.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify three stakeholders for a radio-enabled circuit and write a different testable concern for each.

courses.title: Logic Design
courses.rationale: Discuss how digital logic behaves for users, maintainers, and downstream system designers.

stakeholders.name: End users
stakeholders.need: Predictable behavior when inputs or timing vary
stakeholders.why: They depend on the digital output behaving predictably even after reset or invalid input.

stakeholders.name: Digital designers
stakeholders.why: They define the logic and interface assumptions that determine system behavior.

stakeholders.name: Verification engineers
stakeholders.why: They need observable states to verify both intended behavior and faults.

stakeholders.name: System integrators
stakeholders.why: They combine blocks from different sources and are affected by undocumented interfaces.

factors.consideration: A wrong logic state can propagate to a safety-critical output in some applications.
factors.implication: Define a safe default and test invalid inputs where relevant.
factors.example: An invalid state energizes an actuator output.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a state table to identify invalid inputs and safer default outputs.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to add a safe default to a finite-state design and show a test that reaches the invalid state.

factors.consideration: Unexpected state transitions reduce dependable system behavior.
factors.implication: Specify reset and recovery behavior.
factors.example: A reset produces a brief wrong output that interrupts a downstream device.
factors.teachingIdea: Simulate reset and recovery before comparing implementations.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to explain a reset glitch and specify observable recovery behavior for a dependent user.

factors.consideration: Reusable blocks may lower redesign and verification effort.
factors.implication: Record interface assumptions and reuse costs.
factors.example: A reusable logic block saves redesign time but needs interface and verification work.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare reuse with a fresh design using a small effort estimate.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose reuse or redesign for a logic module, accounting for verification and integration cost.

factors.consideration: Shared hardware description practices support collaboration across teams.
factors.implication: Use a documented language and interface convention.
factors.example: Two teams interpret the same HDL interface differently.
factors.teachingIdea: Have teams exchange a short interface description and identify ambiguity.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to revise an ambiguous digital interface specification so an external team can implement it consistently.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Trace one invalid input through a logic block and ask who notices the resulting output.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to map an invalid-state concern from an end user to a verification test.

courses.title: Signals and Systems
courses.rationale: Relate signal quality and numerical assumptions to decisions made from measurements.

stakeholders.name: Measurement users
stakeholders.need: Signals with known accuracy and limitations
stakeholders.why: They act on a signal or measurement and need to know its uncertainty.

stakeholders.name: Signal-processing engineers
stakeholders.why: They choose sampling and processing assumptions that may preserve or lose information.

stakeholders.name: System operators
stakeholders.why: They rely on timely detection of a meaningful signal change.

stakeholders.name: People affected by automated decisions
stakeholders.need: Awareness of false alarms or missed events
stakeholders.why: A false alarm or missed event can directly affect their experience or treatment.

factors.consideration: Noise or sampling errors can hide a signal needed for service continuity.
factors.implication: Set signal-to-noise and sampling assumptions before interpreting results.
factors.example: A low sampling rate makes a fast event appear as a slower signal.
factors.teachingIdea: Plot the same signal at two sampling rates and compare interpretations.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose a sampling rate for a given signal and explain how aliasing could mislead a service operator.

factors.consideration: A missed transient may delay a protective response in an applied system.
factors.implication: Check detection delay and false-negative behavior.
factors.example: A short transient is missed by a detector that averages over too long a window.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare detection delay and noise rejection for two time windows.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to select a detection window and justify the safety trade-off between false alarms and missed transients.

factors.consideration: Higher sampling and processing rates increase equipment and energy costs.
factors.implication: Choose a rate justified by the information needed.
factors.example: A faster ADC and processor cost more than the application needs.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare data quality and system cost for two sampling configurations.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose an ADC rate for a stated signal and justify why extra resolution or speed is or is not worth its cost.

factors.consideration: Signal-based decisions may affect people when uncertainty is hidden.
factors.implication: Communicate confidence and limitations with the reported result.
factors.example: A sensor dashboard presents a noisy estimate as a precise fact.
factors.teachingIdea: Discuss how uncertainty should appear in a user-facing signal report.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to rewrite a sensor alert to communicate uncertainty without hiding an important event.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Show a sampled signal and ask who would be affected if its peak were missed.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify two users of a sensor signal and explain how sampling error changes each user's decision.

courses.title: Electrical Machines
courses.rationale: Examine machine operation from the perspectives of operators, maintenance staff, energy users, and facility owners.

stakeholders.name: Machine operators
stakeholders.why: They start, stop, and supervise the machine and face the consequences of unexpected operation.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance personnel
stakeholders.why: They inspect insulation and mechanical parts and need safe access to identify faults.

stakeholders.name: Facility owners
stakeholders.why: They pay for outages, energy, and replacement over the machine's life.

stakeholders.name: Nearby workers
stakeholders.need: Protection from heat, noise, and moving parts
stakeholders.why: They may be exposed to moving parts, noise, or heat without operating the machine.

stakeholders.name: Equipment manufacturers
stakeholders.why: They need a clear duty cycle and testable performance expectations.

factors.consideration: Rotating parts, overheating, and insulation faults can harm people or equipment.
factors.implication: Specify guards, thermal limits, and a fault shutdown condition.
factors.example: A motor shaft is accessible while the machine can start unexpectedly.
factors.teachingIdea: Walk through a machine startup and maintenance scenario.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify a rotating-part and insulation hazard and specify a guard or shutdown requirement.

factors.consideration: Machine outages may interrupt a dependent facility process.
factors.implication: Define availability and maintenance intervals.
factors.example: A pump motor outage interrupts water delivery to a facility.
factors.teachingIdea: Map the machine to the service it supports.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set an availability or maintenance requirement for a motor serving a critical pump.

factors.consideration: Machine losses increase electricity use and cooling needs.
factors.implication: Compare efficiency at expected load points.
factors.example: Two motors have different efficiency at the facility's usual partial load.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare efficiency curves at realistic operating points.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to calculate annual electricity use for two motors at the expected load and explain the environmental consequence.

factors.consideration: Purchase price alone may understate energy and maintenance cost.
factors.implication: Evaluate total ownership cost over a realistic duty cycle.
factors.example: A cheaper motor costs more to operate and repair over five years.
factors.teachingIdea: Build a simple purchase-plus-energy-plus-maintenance comparison.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between two machines using lifecycle cost rather than purchase price alone.

factors.consideration: Noise and heat exposure may matter in occupied or industrial spaces.
factors.implication: Measure or estimate exposure in the intended setting.
factors.example: A machine adds heat and noise near an occupied work area.
factors.teachingIdea: Discuss what should be measured at the actual installation.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose one measurement and one design change for a noisy or overheated machine room.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Use a pump-motor example and ask what operators, nearby workers, and maintenance staff need from the same design.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to derive separate operating and maintenance requirements for an industrial motor installation.

courses.title: Power Electronics
courses.rationale: Use a converter design to consider hazards, power quality, energy loss, and lifecycle cost.

stakeholders.name: Equipment users
stakeholders.why: They depend on converted power meeting the stated output limits.

stakeholders.name: Converter operators
stakeholders.why: They start, stop, and respond to converter faults.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance personnel
stakeholders.why: They may encounter stored charge and need a clear diagnostic path.

stakeholders.name: Utilities
stakeholders.need: Acceptable grid interaction and power quality
stakeholders.why: They share the electrical network and may see harmonics or connection effects.

stakeholders.name: Manufacturers
stakeholders.why: They select parts and thermal design that make the converter feasible.

stakeholders.name: Facility owners
stakeholders.need: Affordable energy and maintenance over service life
stakeholders.why: They bear energy and service costs over the converter lifetime.

stakeholders.name: Nearby equipment users
stakeholders.why: Their equipment can be affected by distortion from a shared bus.

factors.consideration: Electric shock, thermal stress, overcurrent, and insulation failure.
factors.implication: Set isolation, protection, and fault-temperature requirements.
factors.example: A DC-link capacitor remains charged after the converter is switched off.
factors.teachingIdea: Walk through the stored-energy and fault paths on a converter schematic.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to specify an isolation or discharge requirement and a way to verify safe maintenance access.

factors.consideration: Converter failure can interrupt supplied equipment.
factors.implication: Specify acceptable output quality and recovery behavior.
factors.example: An output sag from the converter stops a production process.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare output waveforms under normal and fault conditions.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to define an output-voltage and recovery criterion for a converter supplying a sensitive load.

factors.consideration: Converter losses, cooling energy, and end-of-life electronics.
factors.implication: Set a rated-load efficiency target and consider replaceable parts.
factors.example: One converter is 94% efficient and another 97% efficient at rated load.
factors.teachingIdea: Calculate losses and cooling demand for two designs at the same output power.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare two converter efficiencies and explain effects on energy use, cooling, operating cost, and environmental impact.

factors.consideration: Efficiency and repairability affect energy and lifecycle cost.
factors.implication: Compare purchase, operation, and maintenance costs.
factors.example: A smaller heat sink cuts purchase cost but raises cooling and repair expense.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare initial and operating costs using a simple duty cycle.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between two converter thermal designs using lifecycle cost and an explicit assumption about operating hours.

factors.consideration: A grid-connected converter may need interoperable connection behavior.
factors.implication: Define an appropriate interface and verification plan.
factors.example: A grid-tied converter must connect predictably to a shared network.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a short connection scenario to discuss interface behavior.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify one grid-interface requirement and explain how a different deployment setting might change it.

factors.consideration: Harmonic distortion can affect other connected users.
factors.implication: Measure or estimate harmonics at the shared connection.
factors.example: Converter harmonics disturb another user on the same electrical bus.
factors.teachingIdea: Show a harmonic spectrum and identify affected loads.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify who is affected by converter harmonics and propose a measurement or mitigation informed by IEEE 519.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Draw a converter connected to a shared bus and ask who experiences a fault, loss, or harmonic distortion.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify the utility, operator, and neighboring equipment user, then derive one converter requirement for each.

courses.title: Electronic Engineering
courses.rationale: Consider electronic product robustness, compatibility, and the people who use or maintain the device.

stakeholders.name: Product users
stakeholders.need: Reliable operation and clear fault indication
stakeholders.why: They see both normal product behavior and the consequences of failure.

stakeholders.name: RF equipment operators
stakeholders.why: They need the electronic device to work near other radio equipment.

stakeholders.name: Test laboratories
stakeholders.why: They must produce evidence that a robustness claim is repeatable.

stakeholders.name: Repair technicians
stakeholders.why: They need safe access to diagnose and replace failed parts.

stakeholders.name: Nearby device users
stakeholders.why: They depend on a compatible electromagnetic environment.

factors.consideration: Component faults may cause overheating or unstable outputs.
factors.implication: Specify a safe response to a representative component fault.
factors.example: A shorted output device overheats an amplifier enclosure.
factors.teachingIdea: Trace a single-component fault and its thermal path.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to specify a fault-detection or shutdown response for an overheating amplifier.

factors.consideration: RF susceptibility can interrupt intended product behavior.
factors.implication: Set an immunity test for the expected environment.
factors.example: A nearby radio source causes an electronic product to reset.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a product-EMC case to discuss immunity rather than ideal-circuit behavior.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to define an immunity test and state the maximum acceptable change in product operation.

factors.consideration: Power consumption and component replacement influence device lifetime impact.
factors.implication: Measure active and standby power and consider repair access.
factors.example: A device draws unnecessary standby power throughout its service life.
factors.teachingIdea: Estimate annual standby energy for two design options.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare active and standby energy for two products and justify one change to reduce lifecycle impact.

factors.consideration: Shielding and robustness choices change product cost.
factors.implication: Compare mitigation cost against expected performance.
factors.example: Shielding improves robustness but raises production cost; filtering offers a different trade-off.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare a shielding and filtering option using test results and cost.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose an EMC mitigation strategy for a stated product budget and defend its expected performance.

factors.consideration: Unclear interfaces or failures can exclude or frustrate users.
factors.implication: Test understandable status and recovery information.
factors.example: A user cannot tell whether an indicator means normal operation or a recoverable fault.
factors.teachingIdea: Ask peers to interpret status feedback without documentation.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to redesign a product indicator and explain how the change helps a user recover from a fault.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Use an amplifier near a radio transmitter and list the different concerns of users, repairers, and test staff.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to derive a product test for a user concern and a service requirement for a repair technician.

courses.title: Microprocessors Design
courses.rationale: Use an embedded-system example to connect timing, interfaces, faults, and maintainability to affected users.

stakeholders.name: Embedded-system users
stakeholders.why: They experience a wrong or delayed response from the embedded device.

stakeholders.name: Firmware developers
stakeholders.need: Clear hardware interfaces and timing assumptions
stakeholders.why: They must implement the timing and interface assumptions set by the hardware.

stakeholders.name: System integrators
stakeholders.why: They combine components and need compatible, documented interfaces.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance engineers
stakeholders.why: They need diagnostics and update access after deployment.

stakeholders.name: Sensor-data users
stakeholders.why: They make decisions from sensor values and need accuracy and timing context.

factors.consideration: A processor hang or incorrect output can affect a controlled device.
factors.implication: Define watchdog, reset, and safe-output behavior where needed.
factors.example: A frozen microcontroller leaves a valve command active.
factors.teachingIdea: Inject a watchdog timeout into an embedded-system example.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to design a safe output state for a controller hang and specify a fault-injection test.

factors.consideration: Timing or interface faults reduce service dependability.
factors.implication: State timing bounds and recovery behavior.
factors.example: Sensor timestamps drift and a monitoring system acts on stale data.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare a trace with synchronized and unsynchronized measurements.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set a maximum sensor-data age and explain its consequence for the system user.

factors.consideration: Interoperable component descriptions support integration across suppliers.
factors.implication: Document an interface using a reusable representation.
factors.example: Two suppliers describe the same module interface differently.
factors.teachingIdea: Exchange a brief interface contract between student teams.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify an ambiguous timing or data field and rewrite it for cross-supplier integration.

factors.consideration: Diagnostic access can lower future maintenance cost.
factors.implication: Compare test coverage and service effort.
factors.example: An extra diagnostic port costs more initially but reduces field service visits.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare development cost with expected service effort.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to justify or reject a diagnostic interface using a simple maintenance-cost estimate.

factors.consideration: Automated responses may confuse users without clear status feedback.
factors.implication: Provide a visible fault and recovery state.
factors.example: A device reports faults only through an inaccessible visual signal.
factors.teachingIdea: Review alternative feedback for users with different needs.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose two ways an embedded device could communicate the same critical fault to users.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Trace a sensor reading through firmware to an output and ask who notices a late or wrong response.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to derive one timing requirement for a user and one diagnostic requirement for a maintainer.

courses.title: Control Systems
courses.rationale: Connect controller performance and sensor uncertainty to people operating or depending on the controlled process.

stakeholders.name: Process operators
stakeholders.why: They intervene when the controller behaves unexpectedly.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance engineers
stakeholders.why: They calibrate sensors and diagnose failures in the loop.

stakeholders.name: People near controlled equipment
stakeholders.why: They may be exposed to uncontrolled motion or process conditions.

stakeholders.name: Facility owners
stakeholders.need: Continuity of service and manageable costs
stakeholders.why: They depend on continuous, efficient operation.

stakeholders.name: Sensor-data users
stakeholders.why: They rely on trustworthy measurements and timestamps.

factors.consideration: Instability, actuator saturation, or sensor failure may create hazardous motion or process states.
factors.implication: Define a safe state and test a representative failure.
factors.example: A poorly tuned controller overshoots the safe travel of an actuator.
factors.teachingIdea: Plot a step response and mark the point where performance becomes hazardous.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set an overshoot limit and describe the safe state after a failed sensor reading.

factors.consideration: Poor response or loss of synchronization can interrupt a service.
factors.implication: Set settling, availability, and timing criteria.
factors.example: Timing drift causes a controller to miss a service target.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare control traces with different delay and synchronization.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to specify settling time and data-timing bounds for a process that users depend on.

factors.consideration: Conservative tuning can trade energy or throughput against performance.
factors.implication: Compare operating cost for candidate control settings.
factors.example: Aggressive control reduces response time but raises energy consumption.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare two tuning settings using response and energy plots.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to justify a tuning choice using both operating cost and control performance.

factors.consideration: Control choices affect process energy and material waste.
factors.implication: Include energy or waste in performance comparison.
factors.example: Repeated overshoot wastes material in a controlled process.
factors.teachingIdea: Estimate waste under two response profiles.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare two controllers and quantify how overshoot changes energy or material use.

factors.consideration: Operator understanding influences safe intervention.
factors.implication: Test whether alarms communicate a useful action.
factors.example: An alarm says only “fault” and gives an operator no useful action.
factors.teachingIdea: Role-play the operator response to two alarm messages.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to rewrite a control alarm so it communicates a specific condition and a safe next action.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Follow a control-loop fault from sensor to actuator and ask whose concern emerges at each step.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to assign one safe-state concern to a nearby person and one recovery concern to an operator.

courses.title: Electromagnetics Fundamental
courses.rationale: Discuss field measurement, exposure, propagation, and spectrum sharing in an applied electromagnetic example.

stakeholders.name: RF equipment users
stakeholders.why: They rely on radio performance and may be near the device in normal use.

stakeholders.name: People near installations
stakeholders.why: They may be near an antenna site without operating the equipment.

stakeholders.name: Spectrum regulators
stakeholders.why: They need evidence that radio operation fits assigned bands and constraints.

stakeholders.name: Nearby spectrum users
stakeholders.why: They can experience interference from a new installation.

stakeholders.name: Field technicians
stakeholders.why: They measure fields and need safe procedures near energized equipment.

stakeholders.name: Communities near sites
stakeholders.why: They experience local coverage, siting, and communication effects.

factors.consideration: RF exposure can matter near a transmitter or during maintenance.
factors.implication: Estimate exposure for the stated scenario and compare it with an appropriate limit.
factors.example: A technician approaches a transmitting antenna while measuring a field.
factors.teachingIdea: Work a field-exposure scenario and distinguish estimated exposure from assumed harm.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to estimate a field or exposure for a stated setup and explain when comparison with IEEE C95.1 is appropriate.

factors.consideration: Measurement setup or high-field operation can expose technicians to hazards.
factors.implication: Define separation and shutdown procedures for testing.
factors.example: A measurement is attempted before the transmitter is isolated.
factors.teachingIdea: Discuss a safe field-measurement plan near energized equipment.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose separation, shutdown, and verification steps for an antenna measurement.

factors.consideration: Site placement and equipment energy use may affect the surrounding area.
factors.implication: Compare placement and power choices for the application.
factors.example: Two antenna locations have different power demand and local siting effects.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare sites using coverage and operating-energy assumptions.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare two site choices and justify one using propagation, energy, and local environmental effects.

factors.consideration: Radio systems may cross borders or share internationally allocated bands.
factors.implication: State the operating band and interoperability assumption.
factors.example: A radio device designed for one band is proposed for use in another country.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare band and equipment assumptions in two deployment settings.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to explain why a radio design cannot automatically be deployed unchanged under a different band allocation.

factors.consideration: Coverage gaps may affect access to a useful radio service.
factors.implication: Map coverage for affected users or locations.
factors.example: A street-level coverage gap affects one neighborhood more than another.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a simple propagation map to identify who lacks service.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify affected users on a coverage map and propose one engineering change to improve service.

factors.consideration: Propagation loss can reduce service availability.
factors.implication: Set a link margin for the expected environment.
factors.example: Rain or path loss reduces the margin of a radio link.
factors.teachingIdea: Build a link budget for two propagation conditions.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to calculate a link margin and explain how a low margin affects service availability.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Sketch an antenna site and ask who is affected by exposure, coverage, measurement work, and spectrum use.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify four stakeholders around a proposed antenna site and derive one distinct concern for each.

courses.title: Communication Systems
courses.rationale: Use a broadcast or mobile link to examine who receives service, who shares spectrum, and how reliability is evidenced.

stakeholders.name: End users
stakeholders.why: They depend on coverage, usable data rates, and continuity of communication.

stakeholders.name: Broadcasters
stakeholders.why: They need predictable signal quality for their audience.

stakeholders.name: Mobile and network operators
stakeholders.why: They plan capacity and must keep service available at manageable cost.

stakeholders.name: Spectrum regulators
stakeholders.why: They allocate spectrum and manage interference among services.

stakeholders.name: Equipment manufacturers
stakeholders.why: They build radios that must interoperate with network interfaces.

stakeholders.name: Emergency services
stakeholders.why: They may depend on communication when other infrastructure fails.

stakeholders.name: Nearby spectrum users
stakeholders.why: They lose service when another transmitter causes harmful interference.

stakeholders.name: Communities receiving service
stakeholders.why: They experience both coverage and gaps in access to the service.

factors.consideration: RF exposure may matter for an installation or operating scenario.
factors.implication: Identify when an exposure assessment is needed; do not assume one for every link.
factors.example: A rooftop base station raises an exposure question for nearby people and workers.
factors.teachingIdea: Discuss when an RF exposure estimate is needed, distinguishing it from a coverage calculation.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify the operating facts needed before deciding whether an RF exposure assessment is relevant.

factors.consideration: Unreliable emergency communication or harmful interference can affect safety.
factors.implication: Define a service-availability or interference constraint.
factors.example: Interference interrupts an emergency radio link during a local incident.
factors.teachingIdea: Use a short outage case to discuss failure and interference paths.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose an interference or availability requirement for emergency communication and explain who it protects.

factors.consideration: Coverage and network reliability influence continuity of communication.
factors.implication: Set a coverage and outage target for the intended users.
factors.example: A coverage gap leaves users without a dependable mobile service.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare a coverage map with a network availability target.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set a coverage or outage criterion and explain its consequence for a named user group.

factors.consideration: Spectrum allocation and radio interfaces have international context.
factors.implication: Record band and interoperability assumptions.
factors.example: A wireless system uses a band assigned differently in another country.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare spectrum allocation and interface assumptions across two countries.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to explain why a wireless system designed for one frequency allocation cannot automatically be deployed unchanged in another country, and identify affected stakeholders.

factors.consideration: Coverage gaps can deepen digital exclusion.
factors.implication: Compare service reach across affected communities.
factors.example: An outlying community receives weaker service than a central district.
factors.teachingIdea: Discuss a map of coverage and the everyday activities affected by a gap.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare service reach for two communities and propose one engineering option to reduce the gap.

factors.consideration: Spectrum efficiency and infrastructure cost constrain deployment.
factors.implication: Compare capacity, equipment, and deployment cost.
factors.example: A high-capacity site serves more users but costs more to install and operate.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare two network layouts using capacity and cost estimates.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between a new tower and smaller cells using capacity, deployment, and operating cost.

factors.consideration: Transmitters and base stations use energy and create equipment waste.
factors.implication: Estimate energy demand and equipment replacement over service life.
factors.example: Two base-station designs deliver similar coverage with different power demand.
factors.teachingIdea: Estimate annual site energy for two equipment options.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare site energy and equipment replacement over a stated service life.

factors.consideration: Language and local communication habits may affect service acceptance.
factors.implication: Test an interface or message format with intended users.
factors.example: An emergency message is technically delivered but misunderstood in the local language.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare message wording or interface choices with intended users.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to revise an emergency alert for a specified community and propose a way to test comprehension.

factors.consideration: Service affordability and rural/urban infrastructure differ.
factors.implication: Compare coverage and cost for groups with different access constraints.
factors.example: A rural area has sparse towers and lower customer density than an urban area.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare the infrastructure needed to serve two locations.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to propose a coverage plan for rural and urban groups and explain how affordability and infrastructure change the engineering decision.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Draw a shared-spectrum communication network and label users, operators, regulators, emergency services, and neighboring systems.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify four stakeholders in a radio deployment and derive a different coverage, interference, or reliability requirement from each concern.

courses.title: Power Systems
courses.rationale: Use a grid or distribution decision to examine public service, fault response, cost, and uneven impacts.

stakeholders.name: Electricity customers
stakeholders.why: They rely on affordable electricity and experience outages directly.

stakeholders.name: Utility operators
stakeholders.why: They make switching and restoration decisions under changing conditions.

stakeholders.name: Line and substation workers
stakeholders.why: They face hazards from energized lines, faults, and incorrect isolation.

stakeholders.name: Facility owners
stakeholders.why: They may lose production when power quality deteriorates.

stakeholders.name: Distributed-generation owners
stakeholders.why: They need predictable technical conditions for connecting generation.

stakeholders.name: Communities near infrastructure
stakeholders.why: They experience local siting effects and service outcomes.

stakeholders.name: Regulators
stakeholders.why: They need evidence that grid operation meets applicable obligations.

factors.consideration: Faults and energized infrastructure create risks to workers and the public.
factors.implication: Define protection and isolation behavior for a fault case.
factors.example: A feeder fault leaves a line energized while a crew is preparing repair work.
factors.teachingIdea: Trace protection and isolation on a one-line diagram.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify a fault-clearing and isolation requirement that protects workers and the public.

factors.consideration: Outages and poor power quality affect essential services.
factors.implication: Set continuity and power-quality criteria.
factors.example: A clinic loses power during a distribution outage.
factors.teachingIdea: Connect a reliability metric to an essential service rather than treating it as an abstract number.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set an interruption limit for a feeder serving a clinic and explain what happens when the limit is exceeded.

factors.consideration: Transmission losses and equipment choices influence resource use.
factors.implication: Compare loss and equipment lifecycle impacts.
factors.example: A network reinforcement option lowers line losses but uses additional equipment.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare expected losses and equipment lifecycle effects.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare two network options using energy losses and material or replacement impacts.

factors.consideration: Capital and maintenance costs affect long-term utility decisions.
factors.implication: Compare alternatives using lifecycle cost.
factors.example: A substation upgrade costs more initially but avoids repeated repair and outage expense.
factors.teachingIdea: Build a simple lifecycle-cost comparison.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to choose between two investment options using capital, maintenance, and outage cost over a stated horizon.

factors.consideration: Outage burden and affordability may differ across customer groups.
factors.implication: Examine who benefits from a proposed investment and who bears its costs.
factors.example: A remote community has fewer network alternatives and higher reinforcement cost per customer.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare urban and remote service options with the same reliability target.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare network-reinforcement options for an urban and a remote community and discuss how cost, reliability, and infrastructure availability affect the engineering decision.

factors.consideration: Infrastructure changes can affect nearby communities and service expectations.
factors.implication: Identify a communication and feedback need for affected residents.
factors.example: A new line route passes near homes while improving service elsewhere.
factors.teachingIdea: Map beneficiaries and nearby affected residents.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify who gains and who bears local effects from a proposed route and propose one communication or design response.

factors.consideration: Grid-connected resources may depend on interoperable technical practices.
factors.implication: State the connection and verification requirements.
factors.example: Distributed generation must connect without destabilizing a shared grid.
factors.teachingIdea: Read a connection scenario and identify interface assumptions.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to derive one interconnection test or constraint for a proposed distributed resource.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Use a feeder diagram to ask who is affected by a fault, an outage, or an investment decision.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify customers, workers, operators, and a nearby community for a feeder project and derive one requirement from each concern.

courses.title: Senior Design Project
courses.rationale: Start with the actual project and identify affected parties before deciding which contextual dimensions apply. Connect each selected concern to a requirement, relevant standard, and evidence.

stakeholders.name: Client or sponsor
stakeholders.need: A solution that addresses the agreed problem
stakeholders.why: They define the problem and decide whether the delivered solution is useful.

stakeholders.name: End users
stakeholders.why: They live with the design's usability, accessibility, and reliability.

stakeholders.name: Operators
stakeholders.why: They control the system in ordinary and abnormal conditions.

stakeholders.name: Maintenance personnel
stakeholders.why: They maintain the solution after the project team has moved on.

stakeholders.name: Manufacturers
stakeholders.why: They determine whether the design can be built and sourced repeatedly.

stakeholders.name: Regulators
stakeholders.why: They may set constraints or require evidence for the intended application.

stakeholders.name: Surrounding community
stakeholders.why: They may experience site, noise, access, or other local effects.

stakeholders.name: Future users
stakeholders.why: They depend on support, repair, and adaptability over time.

stakeholders.name: Project team
stakeholders.need: Clear responsibilities, risks, and verification evidence
stakeholders.why: They must turn concerns into requirements and evidence within available time.

factors.consideration: Could normal use or foreseeable misuse affect human health?
factors.implication: Define an exposure or health-related limit if the project warrants one.
factors.example: A wearable prototype uses a battery near the body for long periods.
factors.teachingIdea: Ask teams to identify a plausible health exposure before choosing a test.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify a health concern in their project and write a measurable limit or verification method if the concern applies.

factors.consideration: What hazardous states, faults, or failures could harm people or property?
factors.implication: Record a safe-state requirement and verification evidence.
factors.example: A small robot could move unexpectedly after a sensor failure.
factors.teachingIdea: Run a brief hazard walk-through of a project prototype.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to define a safe state after one credible fault and show how they would test it.

factors.consideration: Who depends on availability, accessibility, or reliable operation?
factors.implication: Set usability and service-continuity requirements.
factors.example: An assistive device stops working when its battery is depleted.
factors.teachingIdea: Trace the user activity that depends on the prototype.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to set an availability or low-battery warning requirement tied to a named user need.

factors.consideration: Will the solution cross borders, suppliers, or technical interfaces?
factors.implication: State interoperability and lifecycle assumptions.
factors.example: A module from one supplier must integrate with hardware built elsewhere.
factors.teachingIdea: Map interfaces and supply assumptions for two component sources.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify an interoperability or supply-chain risk and derive a design constraint.

factors.consideration: Could language, practice, or local expectations change acceptance?
factors.implication: Test a user-facing choice with the intended community.
factors.example: A user interface uses language or conventions unfamiliar to intended users.
factors.teachingIdea: Test a prototype message with a representative user or peer role.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to revise one project interface for a specified user group and propose a comprehension test.

factors.consideration: Could the design change access, inclusion, work, or community experience?
factors.implication: Record affected groups and a feedback method.
factors.example: A public kiosk is difficult to use for people with limited mobility or access.
factors.teachingIdea: Map who can and cannot use a proposed prototype.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify an excluded user group and derive one accessible design requirement.

factors.consideration: What energy, material, waste, or site effects occur over the lifecycle?
factors.implication: Compare lifecycle impacts of design alternatives.
factors.example: A disposable battery pack creates recurring waste.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare two powering options across the prototype lifecycle.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to compare battery replacement, energy use, and disposal for two project alternatives.

factors.consideration: Can the solution be built, operated, repaired, and replaced affordably?
factors.implication: Estimate total cost across the expected service life.
factors.example: A low-cost prototype needs expensive maintenance after deployment.
factors.teachingIdea: Build a bill-of-materials plus service-cost comparison.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to estimate total ownership cost and justify one design change that reduces long-term expense.

factors.consideration: Could costs and benefits fall unevenly across groups or locations?
factors.implication: Identify affordability and access constraints for affected groups.
factors.example: A solution works technically but is unaffordable where it is most needed.
factors.teachingIdea: Compare access, infrastructure, and cost for two user groups.
factors.assessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify who receives the benefit and who bears the cost, then derive an affordability or access constraint.

courses.stakeholderTeachingIdea: Map the chain: Stakeholder → Need / Concern → Contextual Factor → Engineering Implication → Requirement / Constraint → Standard → Evidence.
courses.stakeholderAssessmentPrompt: You may ask students to identify at least four stakeholders for their project and derive one testable engineering requirement or constraint from the concern of each stakeholder.
